title: Sampling Distributions: t, Chi-square, F and the Correlation Coefficient
breadcrumb: Probability → Sampling distributions → t, chi-square, F and the correlation coefficient
engineName: Probability — the distributions a statistic follows, and what they are built from
objectives: Build chi-square, t and F from sums of squares of normals and use the identity t² = F(1, k).
Write the exact null density of r and read its shape from the exponent (n − 4)/2.
Derive the n = 3 arcsine and n = 4 uniform results from one symmetric Beta.
Run the exact t test of ρ = 0 and convert it into a critical value for |r|.
Explain the skew of r as ρ → 1 and its degeneracy at ρ = ±1.
Build and interpret a Fisher-z confidence interval for ρ, including its asymmetry.

prereq.name: The normal distribution and sums of squares
prereq.why: All four distributions in this lesson are functions of sums of squares of independent normals.

prereq.name: Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

prereq.name: The Beta distribution
prereq.why: The small-n results are one symmetric Beta seen at three parameter values, which is the economical way to hold them.

traps: The distribution of r is NOT non-degenerate for every population — at ρ = ±1 it collapses to a point.
As ρ → 1 the distribution of r becomes more skewed, not more normal.
Fisher's z has variance 1/(n − 3), not 1/(n − 1) or 1/n.
The exact t test covers only ρ = 0; it cannot test ρ = ρ₀ ≠ 0 or give an interval.
The degrees of freedom are n − 2, not n − 1: a mean was fitted for each variable.
A confidence interval for ρ is NOT symmetric about r; back-transform each endpoint with tanh.
r = 0 means no linear association, not independence.
At n = 4 the 5% critical |r| is 0.95 — a large r from a tiny sample is not evidence.

sheet: χ²ₖ is a sum of k squared standard normals; t_k = Z/√(V/k); F(k₁,k₂) = (U/k₁)/(V/k₂); t_k² = F(1,k).
Exact null density of r: f(r) = [Γ((n−1)/2)/(√π Γ((n−2)/2))] (1 − r²)^((n−4)/2) on (−1, 1).
The exponent (n−4)/2 decides the shape: negative at n = 3 (U-shaped), zero at n = 4 (flat), positive from n = 5.
One substitution covers them all: (1 + r)/2 ~ Beta((n−2)/2, (n−2)/2).
n = 3 → arcsine, f(r) = 1/(π√(1 − r²)). n = 4 → Uniform(−1, 1), f(r) = ½. n = 5 → semicircle, f(r) = (2/π)√(1 − r²).
Exact test of ρ = 0: t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) on n − 2 df.
Worked: n = 12, r = 0.6 → t = 2.3717 on 10 df, two-sided p = 0.0392, critical |r| = 0.5760.
Fisher: z = ½ln((1+r)/(1−r)) = arctanh r, approximately N(arctanh ρ, 1/(n − 3)).
Interval for ρ: transform, z ± 1.96/√(n − 3), back-transform with tanh each endpoint.
Worked: n = 12, r = 0.6 → z = 0.6931, se = 1/3, z-interval (0.0398, 1.3465), ρ-interval (0.0398, 0.8732) — asymmetric, 0.560 below r and 0.273 above.
Skew of r at n = 12: about 0 at ρ = 0, −0.8 at ρ = 0.5, −2.1 at ρ = 0.9. Skew of z at ρ = 0.9: about +0.03.
ρ = ±1 ⟹ r degenerate at ±1, and z is then undefined.
r² = b_yx · b_xy, with r taking the sign the two slopes share.
r = 0 means no LINEAR association; independence only follows under bivariate normality, and from ρ = 0.
Geometry: r = cos θ between the centred vectors; the density exponent is a dimension count, d = n − 1.
Partial correlation controlling for k variables: exact t on n − k − 2 df.
cards: Intervals for ρ, testing ρ₀ ≠ 0, comparing two correlations
More skewed, not more normal — the boundary at 1 compresses it
r degenerate at ±1; the distribution is a single point
r² = b_yx · b_xy, sign shared by the slopes
tricks: Read the shape off the exponent (n − 4)/2 rather than memorising three separate densities.
Convert the critical t into a critical |r| once per sample size: |r|crit = t*/√(n − 2 + t*²).
At n = 4 the null is uniform, so the two-sided p-value is just 1 − |r|.
Check the degrees of freedom by counting fitted parameters: two means fitted, so n − 2.
If a question mentions an interval for ρ, or any ρ₀ other than zero, it wants Fisher's z.
A negative r with two positive slopes is impossible — both slopes carry the sign of the covariance.
shortcuts: √(1 − r²) is clean at r = 0.6 (= 0.8) and r = 0.8 (= 0.6), which is why exam questions favour them.
arctanh(0.6) = ½ ln 4 = 0.6931; the standard error at n = 12 is exactly 1/3.
For a quick sense of precision, the z-interval half-width is 1.96/√(n − 3) — about 0.65 at n = 12 and 0.36 at n = 30.
remember: A large r from a tiny sample is not evidence; at n = 4 you need |r| > 0.95.
Skew grows as ρ → 1, because there is a wall at 1.
Variance of z is 1/(n − 3). The t test is for ρ = 0 only.

howto: Section 2's interactive chart is the heart of this lesson — move n from 3 upwards and watch the density pass from U-shaped through flat to bell-like, then move ρ and watch the skew build. Those three movements ARE the four statements of the exam question, so spend time there before reading the algebra. Sections 3 and 4 give the exact density and the exact t test; section 6 is June 2026's question itself, ruled on statement by statement. Section 7 is the one most often skipped and most often needed: Fisher's z, and why a confidence interval for ρ is asymmetric. If short of time, sections 2, 3, 6 and 7 are the lesson. The optional section derives the whole thing geometrically — r is the cosine of an angle, and the small-sample results become properties of uniform directions in a plane and on a sphere, which is far easier to retain than three memorised densities.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Fix the three classical sampling distributions as built objects, and settle what r is.

ask.q: t, chi-square and F are all built from normal samples. What single ingredient do all three use?
ask.nudge: Look at what sits under every square root and in every denominator: a sum of squares.

body: A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic — not of the data. The three classical ones all come from the same raw material: sums of squares of independent standard normals.

Chi-square IS such a sum. t is a standard normal divided by the square root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom. F is a ratio of two independent chi-squares, each over its own degrees of freedom. Nothing else is involved.

This lesson adds a fourth statistic to that family, and it is the one the June 2026 paper asked about: the sample correlation coefficient r. Its distribution looks exotic — U-shaped at n = 3, perfectly flat at n = 4 — and yet the exact test for ρ = 0 is an ordinary t test. Both facts come out of the same construction.
Four checks before starting.

items.ask: If X₁, …, Xₙ are independent N(μ, σ²), what is the distribution of (n − 1)s²/σ²?
items.recall: Chi-square with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
refresh: The sample variance, scaled this way, is a sum of squares of n independent normals with one linear constraint — the deviations sum to zero — and each constraint costs one degree of freedom.
It is also independent of the sample mean when the data are normal. That independence is what makes the t statistic work, and it holds only for the normal distribution.
Degrees of freedom are not a convention here; they count the free directions left after the constraints.

items.ask: How is a t random variable with k degrees of freedom built?
items.recall: t = Z / √(V/k), where Z ~ N(0, 1) and V ~ χ²ₖ are independent.
refresh: A standard normal divided by the square root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom. Estimating the scale instead of knowing it is exactly what replaces the normal by the t.
It is symmetric about zero, with heavier tails than the normal, and it approaches the normal as k grows because V/k concentrates at 1.
Section 5 derives the exact test for ρ = 0 and it turns out to be precisely this object with k = n − 2.

items.ask: How is an F random variable built, and what are its two parameters?
items.recall: F = (U/k₁)/(V/k₂), with U ~ χ²ₖ₁ and V ~ χ²ₖ₂ independent; k₁ and k₂ are the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom.
refresh: A ratio of two independent chi-squares, each divided by its own degrees of freedom. The order matters: F(k₁, k₂) is not F(k₂, k₁), and the reciprocal of one is the other.
The square of a t with k degrees of freedom is an F(1, k). That identity is why a two-sided t test and the corresponding F test always agree.
F is non-negative and right-skewed, and it is the test statistic of analysis of variance and of every comparison of nested linear models.

items.ask: What are the bounds on the sample correlation coefficient r, and what forces them?
refresh: r is the inner product of two centred data vectors divided by the product of their lengths — a cosine. Cauchy–Schwarz says a cosine cannot exceed 1 in modulus.

Those hard boundaries are the whole source of the strange behaviour in this lesson. A statistic trapped in a finite interval cannot stay symmetric as its mean approaches an endpoint, which is why the distribution of r skews as ρ approaches 1.

The cosine reading also explains the small-sample results: with n = 3 there are only two free directions after centring, and the angle between two random vectors in a plane is uniform — which is exactly the arcsine law for its cosine.

scenes.title: Why r behaves badly when samples are small
scenes.objective: See that the distribution of r changes shape with n, before any formula.
body: Most statistics behave more or less normally once the sample is reasonably large, and r is no exception: with n = 30 and no real association, r clusters around zero in a recognisable bell.

Small samples are different, and they are different in a way that is easy to state and hard to believe. With n = 4 pairs and no association at all, every value of r between −1 and 1 is exactly as likely as every other: r is uniform on (−1, 1). With n = 3 it is worse than uniform — the density is U-shaped, piling up near ±1 and thinnest at zero. A correlation of 0.9 from three pairs is not evidence of anything.
So 'r is close to 1' carries no fixed meaning. It has to be read against n, and at tiny n it means almost nothing.

The second peculiarity appears at the other end. When the true ρ is large, r cannot scatter symmetrically about it, because there is a wall at 1 and no room above. The distribution bunches against the wall and trails off downwards — it becomes skewed. That is the fact the exam question led with, and it is why the raw r is the wrong scale for an interval.

scenario.teaser: A pilot study reports a correlation of 0.97 from four patients and the finding evaporates.
scenario.title: The correlation that was certain to be large
body: A clinical group runs a pilot on four patients, measuring a candidate biomarker against a severity score. The sample correlation comes out at 0.97. The write-up calls the association near-perfect and proposes a full trial on that basis.

A statistician asks the only question that matters: what would r have looked like had there been no association whatsoever? The answer, for n = 4, is that r would have been uniform on (−1, 1) — so the chance of seeing |r| ≥ 0.97 by pure accident is 0.03 at each end, 6% in total. An r of 0.97 from four pairs is barely distinguishable from noise.

Worse, the reasoning that produced the enthusiasm was circular. With n = 4 a large |r| is not surprising under the null, so a large |r| cannot be evidence against the null. The statistic was read as though its null distribution were concentrated near zero, which is the behaviour of a large sample, not a sample of four.

The exact test settles it in one line. With n = 4, the 5% two-sided critical value for |r| is 0.95, so 0.97 just scrapes past significance and nothing more — a p-value near 0.03 on a single underpowered pilot, with no correction for however many biomarkers were screened.
Run the same arithmetic at n = 30 and the critical value falls to 0.361; at n = 12 it is 0.576. The threshold for 'surprising' depends entirely on n, and at small n it sits absurdly high.
The general lesson is that r has no interpretation on its own. Reporting r without n is reporting a number without its units, and the smaller n is, the more misleading the bare figure becomes.
scenario.q: Why is a large |r| from four pairs not evidence of association, when the same value from thirty pairs would be?
scenario.answer: Because evidence is a comparison with what the null predicts, and the null prediction depends on n. At n = 4 the null distribution of r is uniform on (−1, 1), so values near ±1 are as common under no association as any others, and observing one tells you almost nothing. At n = 30 the null distribution is tightly concentrated near zero, so a value of 0.9 would be extraordinary. The same r is strong evidence in one case and no evidence in the other — which is why the critical value, not the value of r, is what has to be checked.

ask.q: At n = 4 the null distribution of r is uniform on (−1, 1). What does that make the 5% two-sided critical value of |r|?
ask.nudge: For a uniform distribution, probability is proportional to length. How much length sits beyond ±c?

scenes.title: Watch the shape change
scenes.objective: Move n and ρ and see the U-shape, the flat case and the skew appear.

viz.caption: The exact null density of r, with the 5% two-sided critical values marked. Raise n from 3 and watch the shape pass from U-shaped through flat to bell-like; then move ρ away from zero to see the skew build against the boundary at 1.

body: Start at n = 3 with ρ = 0. The density is U-shaped: the arcsine law, thinnest at zero and unbounded at ±1. Note the critical value — 0.997, which is to say that nothing short of a near-perfect correlation is significant on three pairs.

Step to n = 4. The curve goes flat: Uniform(−1, 1) exactly, and the critical value is 0.95. These are statements C and D of the exam question, and they are the same fact seen twice — the exponent (n − 4)/2 in the density is negative at n = 3, zero at n = 4 and positive thereafter.
Keep raising n. The density becomes unimodal and tightens around zero, and the critical value drops away: 0.576 at n = 12, 0.361 at n = 30, 0.254 at n = 60.

Now set n to 12 and move ρ up to 0.9. The teal curve is the density of r at that ρ, and it is plainly lopsided — packed against 1 with a tail reaching back down. That is statement A. Push ρ to 0.95 and the asymmetry becomes extreme, which is why an interval of the form r ± something is indefensible at high correlation.

ask.q: The null density is proportional to (1 − r²) raised to the power (n − 4)/2. Why does that single exponent decide whether the curve is U-shaped, flat or peaked?
ask.nudge: At r = 0 the factor (1 − r²) equals 1; near r = ±1 it approaches 0. What does raising a number just below 1 to a negative, zero, or positive power do?

scenes.title: The four distributions, and where r's comes from
scenes.objective: State all four precisely and see that r's exact test is a t test.

blocks.body:
χ²ₖ = Z₁² + … + Zₖ²  with the Zᵢ independent standard normals; mean k, variance 2k.
t_k = Z / √(V/k)  with Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ χ²ₖ independent; symmetric, heavier-tailed than normal.
F(k₁,k₂) = (U/k₁)/(V/k₂)  with U ~ χ²ₖ₁ and V ~ χ²ₖ₂ independent; non-negative, right-skewed.
Two identities worth holding: t_k² = F(1, k), and 1/F(k₁,k₂) = F(k₂,k₁).

blocks.h: The exact null density of r
blocks.body:
For a sample of n pairs from a bivariate normal with ρ = 0,
    f(r) = [Γ((n−1)/2) / (√π · Γ((n−2)/2))] · (1 − r²)^((n−4)/2),  −1 < r < 1.
It is symmetric about zero, and Var(r) = 1/(n − 1) exactly. Everything surprising about small samples is in the exponent (n − 4)/2.

blocks.h: One substitution unifies the special cases
blocks.body:
Put u = (1 + r)/2, mapping (−1, 1) onto (0, 1). Then
    u ~ Beta((n−2)/2, (n−2)/2),
a symmetric Beta. The three cases people memorise separately are three values of one parameter:
  n = 3 → Beta(½, ½), the arcsine law — U-shaped, density 1/(π√(1 − r²)).
  n = 4 → Beta(1, 1), the uniform — density ½ on (−1, 1).
  n = 5 → Beta(1½, 1½), a semicircle — density (2/π)√(1 − r²).
From n = 5 on, the density is unimodal and tends to normality.

blocks.h: The exact test for ρ = 0 is a t test
blocks.body:
Under H₀: ρ = 0,
    t = r √(n − 2) / √(1 − r²)  ~  t_{n−2}.
This is EXACT, not an approximation, and it is the answer to the variant asking for the exact test statistic. Inverting it gives the critical value for r itself:
    |r|crit = t* / √(n − 2 + t*²),  with t* the two-sided critical t on n − 2 df.
At 5%: 0.997 (n = 3), 0.950 (n = 4), 0.576 (n = 12), 0.361 (n = 30), 0.254 (n = 60).

blocks.h: Why it is only a test of ρ = 0
blocks.body: The t form works because the null distribution of r is symmetric and free of nuisance parameters when ρ = 0. For any other ρ the density is skewed and depends on ρ in a way no simple transformation removes exactly, so this statistic cannot test H₀: ρ = ρ₀ for ρ₀ ≠ 0, and cannot give a confidence interval. Section 6 supplies the tool that can.

If ρ = ±1 the two variables are exactly linearly related, every sample lies on a line, and r = ±1 with probability one. The distribution of r is then a single point: degenerate. This is why statement B of the exam question is FALSE — the distribution of r is NOT non-degenerate across the whole range of possibilities, because the endpoints ρ = ±1 collapse it.

ask.nudge: Look at what section 2's visualisation showed when you moved ρ away from zero.

scenes.title: Worked in full — testing a correlation of 0.6 on twelve pairs
scenes.objective: Run the exact test two ways and read the result honestly.

ask.q: The test was significant at 5%, and the critical |r| was 0.576 against an observed 0.6. What does that narrow margin tell you?
ask.nudge: How much would r have to drop for the conclusion to reverse? And how stable is r itself on twelve pairs?

scenes.problem: A sample of n = 12 pairs from an approximately bivariate normal population gives r = 0.6. Test H₀: ρ = 0 against a two-sided alternative at the 5% level, and say how strong the evidence is.

steps.why: Note √(1 − r²) = √0.64 = 0.8 exactly, which keeps the arithmetic clean. The degrees of freedom are n − 2, not n − 1: two parameters were fitted, one for each variable's mean.

steps.say: Compare with the critical value and get the p-value.
steps.math:
t*₀.₉₇₅,₁₀ = 2.2281
2.3717 > 2.2281, so reject H₀ at 5%
two-sided p = 0.0392
steps.why: Significant, but only just. A p-value of 0.039 on a single test is weak evidence by any standard, and would not survive a correction for multiple comparisons.

steps.say: Cross-check by converting the critical t into a critical r.
steps.why: The observed 0.6 exceeds 0.576, which is the same decision reached from the other direction. This form is the useful one in practice — one number per sample size, read straight off against r.

steps.say: State what was and was not established.
steps.math:
r = 0.6, n = 12, t = 2.372 on 10 df, p = 0.039
reject ρ = 0 at 5%; margin above the critical value: 0.024
steps.why: The evidence is against ρ = 0 and that is all. It does not establish that ρ is near 0.6: the margin is 0.024, and section 7 shows the 95% interval for ρ runs from about 0.04 to 0.87 — consistent with almost any positive association.

scenes.after: Two habits from this. First, convert to a critical |r| once per sample size; it makes the dependence on n visible and stops r being read as though 0.6 meant the same thing at every n. Second, rejecting ρ = 0 is a statement about zero, not about the size of ρ — and the interval in section 7 is what settles the second question.

scenes.title: Pause and recall
scenes.objective: Retrieve the constructions before the exam question.

items.q: How is t_k built from a normal and a chi-square?
items.a: t = Z/√(V/k), with Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ χ²ₖ independent.

items.q: What is the exact test statistic for H₀: ρ = 0, and its degrees of freedom?
items.a: t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²), on n − 2 degrees of freedom.

items.q: What is the null distribution of r when n = 4?

items.a: The arcsine distribution, which is U-shaped: density 1/(π√(1 − r²)).

scenes.title: Your turn — June 2026, Q46
scenes.objective: Rule on all four statements and see which two are the trap.
scenes.problem: For a sample of n pairs from a bivariate normal population, rule on each statement about the sampling distribution of r. (A) As the population correlation ρ approaches +1, the distribution of r becomes left-skewed. (B) At ρ = ±1, the distribution of r is non-degenerate. (C) Under ρ = 0, r has a U-shaped arcsine distribution when n = 3. (D) Under ρ = 0, r follows Uniform(−1, 1) when n = 4.

steps.say: Statement A — the shape when the correlation is high.

blank.prompt: True or false, and why in one clause?
blank.answer: True — the boundary at 1 prevents symmetric scatter, so the density skews
blank.hint: There is a hard wall at 1 and no room above it. What must happen to a distribution whose centre approaches a boundary?

steps.why: True. With ρ = 0.9 and n = 12 the simulated skewness of r is about −2.1, against essentially 0 at ρ = 0. The cause is structural: r cannot exceed 1, so as ρ rises the distribution packs against the boundary and trails downward.

steps.say: Statement B — the one that looks harmless.

blank.prompt: True or false, and what case breaks it?
blank.answer: False — at ρ = ±1 the distribution of r is degenerate at ±1
blank.hint: Is there any population for which r takes a single value with probability one?

steps.why: False, and this is the statement that decides the question. If ρ = ±1 the variables lie exactly on a line, so every possible sample gives r = ±1 and the distribution collapses to a point. Marking B as true is what turned the answer into 'B, D only'.

blank.prompt: True or false? Give the density if true.
blank.answer: True — f(r) = 1/(π√(1 − r²)), the arcsine law, U-shaped
blank.hint: Put n = 3 into (1 − r²)^((n−4)/2). What is the exponent?

steps.why: True. At n = 3 the exponent is −½, so the density is proportional to (1 − r²)^(−½), and the constant works out to 1/π. It rises without bound at ±1 and is lowest at 0 — U-shaped.

blank.prompt: True or false? What is the exponent at n = 4?
blank.answer: True — the exponent is 0, so the density is the constant ½ on (−1, 1)
blank.hint: (1 − r²) raised to the power zero is what, for every r?

steps.why: True. The exponent (n − 4)/2 vanishes at n = 4, the density is constant, and normalising over an interval of length 2 gives ½. So r is exactly Uniform(−1, 1).

A, C and D — the official answer. The marked response was 'B, D only', which both rejected the skewness in A and accepted the degeneracy claim in B. Two independent slips, and either one alone would have cost the mark, which is why this lesson teaches A and B as carefully as the eye-catching small-n results in C and D.

scenes.after: The structural point is worth separating from the arithmetic. C and D are memorable curiosities and are easy to recall once seen. A and B are the ones that need understanding: both follow from r living on a closed interval, A because a distribution cannot stay symmetric against a wall, B because at ρ = ±1 the wall is all there is.

scenes.title: Fisher's z — the right scale for an interval
scenes.objective: Know the transformation, its variance, and why it is needed at all.

blocks.body:
z = ½ ln((1 + r)/(1 − r)) = arctanh(r).
Approximately,
    z ~ N( ½ ln((1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ)),  1/(n − 3) ).
The mean is the same transformation applied to ρ, written ζ. The variance 1/(n − 3) does not depend on ρ — which is the entire point.

Two problems with r are fixed at once. Its distribution is skewed when ρ is far from zero, and its variance depends on ρ, shrinking as ρ approaches ±1. The arctanh transformation stretches the ends of (−1, 1) out to the whole real line, which undoes the compression against the boundary: the skew largely disappears and the variance becomes constant. Simulation at n = 12, ρ = 0.9 gives the skewness of r as about −2.1 and of z as about +0.03 — the asymmetry is almost entirely removed.

blocks.h: Building a confidence interval, in three steps
blocks.body:
1. Transform: z = arctanh(r).
2. Interval on the z scale, where normality is reasonable: z ± 1.96/√(n − 3).
3. Transform back with r = tanh(z) to get limits for ρ.
The interval for ρ is NOT symmetric about r, and it should not be. Back-transforming a symmetric interval through a non-linear function is what produces the correct asymmetry.

blocks.h: When z is required and t will not do
blocks.body: Use Fisher's z for a confidence interval for ρ; for testing H₀: ρ = ρ₀ with ρ₀ ≠ 0; and for comparing two independent correlations, where z₁ − z₂ has variance 1/(n₁ − 3) + 1/(n₂ − 3). The exact t test covers only ρ₀ = 0. That division answers the variant asking when z is preferred to t.

The variance is 1/(n − 3), not 1/(n − 1) or 1/n; some texts write 1/(n − 3) for the variance of z and others quote a standard error of 1/√(n − 3) — the same thing. And z is undefined at r = ±1, since arctanh(±1) is infinite, which is the transformation's way of reporting the degeneracy of statement B.

ask.q: The variance of z is 1/(n − 3) regardless of ρ, while the variance of r depends on ρ. Why does that difference matter so much for a confidence interval?
ask.nudge: To build an interval you need the standard error. What would you have to know to compute the standard error of r?

scenes.title: On your own — the interval for ρ
scenes.objective: Build a Fisher-z interval and read its asymmetry correctly.
scenes.problem: With n = 12 and r = 0.6, construct a 95% confidence interval for ρ. (a) Give z and its standard error. (b) Give the interval on the z scale. (c) Back-transform to ρ. (d) Is the interval symmetric about 0.6, and what does its width tell you about the conclusion of section 4?
hints: The standard error is 1/√(n − 3), with n = 12.
Back-transform with tanh, applying it to each endpoint separately.
scenes.answer: (a) z = 0.6931, se = 0.3333. (b) (0.0398, 1.3465). (c) ρ in (0.0398, 0.8732). (d) Not symmetric, and extremely wide — consistent with almost any positive association.
scenes.check: Three things to get exactly right. The standard error is 1/√(12 − 3) = 1/3 = 0.3333, using n − 3 and not n − 1. The lower limit happens to be 0.0398 on both the z scale and the ρ scale, which is a coincidence of tanh being near-identity close to zero, not an error. And the interval is asymmetric about r = 0.6: it reaches 0.273 below and only 0.273… no — it reaches 0.560 below and 0.273 above, so the longer arm points downward, away from the boundary at 1. That asymmetry is the correct answer, not a defect.

scenario.teaser: Two labs report the same correlation and draw opposite conclusions, and both are wrong.
scenario.title: The significant result that excluded almost nothing
body: Two groups measure the same pair of variables. One has twelve observations and gets r = 0.6; the other has two hundred and gets r = 0.6. Both report a significant positive correlation, and both are right about that much.

The first group then describes the association as strong, meaning that ρ is somewhere near 0.6. The interval says otherwise: ρ lies between 0.04 and 0.87 with 95% confidence. That interval excludes zero — just — and excludes essentially nothing else. A ρ of 0.1 and a ρ of 0.85 are both compatible with the data.
The second group's interval, from n = 200, runs from about 0.51 to 0.68. That is a claim about the size of ρ, and it is the claim the first group only appeared to make.

The mistake has a precise shape: treating a rejected null as an estimate. Section 4 rejected ρ = 0 at p = 0.039, which licenses the statement that ρ is probably not zero, and nothing about its magnitude. The two groups had the same point estimate and vastly different information about ρ, and only the interval shows it.

The asymmetry of the first interval carries information too. It extends 0.56 below the estimate and only 0.27 above, because the boundary at 1 compresses the upper side. If a symmetric interval r ± 1.96·se had been quoted instead, the upper limit would have run past what the parameter space allows at larger r — a construction that can produce limits above 1, which is impossible.
Hence the discipline: for a test of ρ = 0 use the exact t; for any statement about the size of ρ transform to z, build the interval there, and bring it back.
scenario.q: Both groups reported r = 0.6 and a significant result. What did the interval reveal that the test could not?
scenario.answer: The test answers one question — is ρ = 0 tenable — and both samples answer it the same way. The interval answers how precisely ρ has been located, and there the samples differ enormously: (0.04, 0.87) from twelve observations against roughly (0.51, 0.68) from two hundred. The first is compatible with a negligible association and with a very strong one; only the second supports a claim about magnitude. A significant p-value says a value has been excluded, not that the estimate is reliable, and with small n a test can reject zero while the interval excludes almost nothing else.

solution.say: (a) Transform r and get the standard error.
solution.why: n − 3 = 9 gives a standard error that is a clean third. Using n − 1 here is the standard slip and would make the interval too narrow.

solution.say: (b) Interval on the z scale, where the normal approximation applies.
solution.why: Symmetric on this scale, because that is the scale on which z is approximately normal with constant variance.
Apply tanh to the endpoints, never to the midpoint and half-width. The lower limit barely moves because tanh is almost the identity near zero; the upper limit is pulled in hard by the boundary at 1.

solution.math:
r = 0.6;  interval (0.0398, 0.8732)
distance below r: 0.560
distance above r: 0.273
width: 0.833
solution.why: Asymmetric, with the longer arm pointing away from the boundary, and so wide as to be almost uninformative about the size of ρ. The section 4 conclusion survives — zero is excluded — but any claim that ρ is near 0.6 does not.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Rule on the claims the variants on this topic are built from.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing any.

items.claim: The exact test of H₀: ρ = 0 uses t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) on n − 2 degrees of freedom.
items.why: True, and exact rather than approximate. The degrees of freedom are n − 2 because a mean was estimated for each of the two variables.

items.claim: r = 0 implies that the two variables are independent.
items.why: False. r = 0 means no LINEAR association in the sample. Y = X² on data symmetric about zero gives a correlation near zero with complete dependence. Only under bivariate normality does zero correlation imply independence, and even then it is zero ρ, not zero r, that does it.

items.claim: The approximate variance of Fisher's z is 1/(n − 3).
items.why: True, and the key feature is that it does not depend on ρ. Simulation at n = 12 gives 0.1107 against 1/9 = 0.1111, and at n = 30 gives 0.0368 against 1/27 = 0.0370.

items.claim: As ρ approaches 1, the distribution of r becomes more nearly normal.
items.why: False — it becomes increasingly skewed, not more normal. The boundary at 1 compresses the upper side: at n = 12 the skewness of r is about 0 at ρ = 0, −0.8 at ρ = 0.5 and −2.1 at ρ = 0.9. This is statement A of the exam question.

items.claim: If ρ = 1 exactly, the distribution of r is degenerate at 1.
items.why: True. An exact linear relationship puts every possible sample on the line, so r = 1 with probability one. This is what makes statement B of the exam question false.

items.claim: r² equals the product of the two regression slopes, b_yx and b_xy.
items.why: True: b_yx = s_xy/s_x², b_xy = s_xy/s_y², and their product is s_xy²/(s_x²s_y²) = r². So r = ±√(b_yx·b_xy), taking the sign the two slopes share — they cannot differ in sign, since both carry the sign of s_xy.

scenes.title: On your own — four quick ones on r
scenes.objective: Apply the small-n results and the slope identity.
scenes.problem: (a) For n = 3 and ρ = 0, give the density of r and name it. (b) For n = 5 and ρ = 0, give the density. (c) If b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45, find r. (d) A study reports r = 0.42 from n = 4 pairs and calls it significant at 5%. Is it?
hints: For (a) and (b), put n into the exponent (n − 4)/2 and then normalise so the density integrates to 1.
For (c), r² is the product of the slopes; the sign is the slopes' shared sign.
For (d), at n = 4 the null distribution of r is uniform on (−1, 1). What is the 5% two-sided critical value?
scenes.answer: (a) 1/(π√(1 − r²)), the arcsine law, U-shaped. (b) (2/π)√(1 − r²), a semicircle. (c) r = +0.6. (d) No — the critical value is 0.95, so 0.42 is nowhere near significance.
scenes.check: On (c), √(0.8 × 0.45) = √0.36 = 0.6, positive because both slopes are. A negative answer would need both slopes negative; one of each sign is impossible. On (d), note how far off the claim is: at n = 4 you need |r| > 0.95, so r = 0.42 has a two-sided p-value of 0.58 — the data are entirely consistent with no association. This is the error from section 2's scenario in reverse: there a large r was over-read, here a moderate one is.

solution.math:
exponent (n − 4)/2 = −½
f(r) ∝ (1 − r²)^(−½)
normalising constant: Γ(1)/(√π Γ(½)) = 1/(√π · √π) = 1/π
f(r) = 1/(π√(1 − r²)),  −1 < r < 1
solution.why: The arcsine distribution, U-shaped: unbounded at ±1 and lowest at 0. Equivalently (1 + r)/2 ~ Beta(½, ½).

solution.math:
exponent = +½
normalising constant: Γ(2)/(√π Γ(3/2)) = 1/(√π · √π/2) = 2/π
f(r) = (2/π)√(1 − r²)
solution.why: A semicircle on (−1, 1) — the first n at which the density is unimodal with a peak at zero. Equivalently (1 + r)/2 ~ Beta(3/2, 3/2).
Both slopes are positive, so r is positive. The identity follows from b_yx = s_xy/s_x² and b_xy = s_xy/s_y².

solution.math:
under ρ = 0 and n = 4, r ~ Uniform(−1, 1)
P(|r| > c) = 1 − c, so the 5% critical value is c = 0.95
0.42 < 0.95 ⟹ not significant;  p = 1 − 0.42 = 0.58
solution.why: Not significant, and by a wide margin. The uniform null makes the p-value almost trivially computable: P(|r| > 0.42) = 1 − 0.42 = 0.58.

scenes.title: Where these four distributions reappear
scenes.objective: Recognise the same constructions across the rest of the syllabus.

blocks.body: Goodness of fit and contingency tables (topics 4.14 and 4.16) compare observed with expected counts through Σ(O − E)²/E; the sampling distribution of a variance is chi-square; and the likelihood ratio test's −2 log λ is asymptotically chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of constraints (topic 4.10).

Every test of a mean or a regression coefficient with an estimated variance, the pivotal quantity behind the classical confidence interval for a mean (topic 4.13), and — as this lesson showed — the exact test for ρ = 0. In each case a normal is divided by the square root of an independent estimated variance.

Analysis of variance, the comparison of nested linear models through the change in residual sum of squares, the test of equality of two variances, and the overall significance test of a regression. The identity t_k² = F(1, k) is why testing a single coefficient by t and by F give the same p-value.

The null density of r reappears as the null distribution of a multiple correlation and of a partial correlation, with the degrees of freedom reduced by the number of variables held constant: a partial correlation controlling for k variables behaves like an ordinary correlation on n − k observations, so the exact t has n − k − 2 degrees of freedom. That is the bridge to topic 8.2.

All four are functions of sums of squares of normals, and all four get their degrees of freedom by counting free directions after constraints. Recognising which sums of squares a statistic is built from is usually faster than recalling its distribution — and it is the only reliable way to get the degrees of freedom right.

ask.q: A partial correlation controls for 2 other variables, computed from n = 20 observations. How many degrees of freedom does its exact t test have?
ask.nudge: An ordinary correlation on n observations gets n − 2. Controlling for k variables costs k more.

scenes.title: Second recall — the parts most likely to fade
scenes.objective: Retrieve Fisher's z and the structural facts.

items.q: Write Fisher's z transformation and its approximate variance.
items.a: z = ½ln((1 + r)/(1 − r)) = arctanh(r), with variance 1/(n − 3).

items.q: When must you use z rather than the exact t?
items.a: For a confidence interval for ρ, for testing ρ = ρ₀ with ρ₀ ≠ 0, and for comparing two independent correlations.

items.q: Why does the distribution of r skew as ρ approaches 1?
items.a: Because r cannot exceed 1, so the distribution compresses against that boundary and trails off downwards.

items.q: What is the distribution of r when ρ = ±1?
items.a: Degenerate at ±1 — every sample gives the same value.

items.q: Express the null distribution of r as a Beta.
items.a: (1 + r)/2 ~ Beta((n − 2)/2, (n − 2)/2), which gives arcsine at n = 3 and uniform at n = 4.
No linear association. Not independence — unless the data are bivariate normal, and even then it is ρ = 0 that gives it.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the mastery test.
body: Build chi-square, t and F from sums of squares of normals, and use t_k² = F(1, k).
Write the exact null density of r and read its shape off the exponent (n − 4)/2.
Give the n = 3 arcsine and n = 4 uniform results, and derive both from (1 + r)/2 ~ Beta((n−2)/2, (n−2)/2).
Run the exact test of ρ = 0 with t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) on n − 2 df, and convert it to a critical |r|.
Explain why r skews as ρ → 1 and why r is degenerate at ρ = ±1.
Build a confidence interval for ρ through Fisher's z with variance 1/(n − 3), and read its asymmetry correctly.
Say what r = 0 does and does not imply, and relate r to the two regression slopes by r² = b_yx·b_xy.

scenes.title: r as a cosine, and where the density comes from
scenes.objective: See the geometric derivation that makes the small-n results obvious rather than exotic.

blocks.body:
Centre both data vectors, giving x̃ and ỹ in ℝⁿ, each lying in the (n − 1)-dimensional subspace orthogonal to the vector of ones. Then
    r = (x̃ · ỹ)/(‖x̃‖‖ỹ‖) = cos θ,
the cosine of the angle between them. Every property of r is a property of that angle.

Under ρ = 0 with normal data, the directions of x̃ and ỹ are independent and uniform on the unit sphere of that (n − 1)-dimensional subspace. The density of the cosine of the angle between two uniform directions in d = n − 1 dimensions is proportional to (1 − r²)^((d−3)/2) = (1 − r²)^((n−4)/2), which is the exact null density. The mysterious exponent is just the dimension count.

n = 3 leaves d = 2: two uniform directions in a PLANE, so the angle between them is uniform on (0, π) and r = cos θ. The cosine of a uniform angle has the arcsine distribution — U-shaped, because a cosine spends most of its time near ±1 and crosses zero quickly. That is statement C, with no integration.
n = 4 leaves d = 3: on a sphere in three dimensions, Archimedes' theorem says the projection onto any axis is uniform — so cos θ is uniform on (−1, 1). That is statement D, and it is the same fact that makes the shadow of a sphere evenly covered.

The cosine reading also explains statement A. Near θ = 0 the cosine is flat — its derivative vanishes — so a spread of angles near zero is squashed into a tiny spread of r values just below 1, while the same spread of angles at θ = π/2 maps to a wide spread of r near zero. A symmetric distribution of angles therefore becomes a skewed distribution of r whenever the angle is small, which is precisely when ρ is near 1. Fisher's arctanh is the function that undoes that squashing.

Three exam facts collapse into one picture: the exponent is a dimension, the n = 3 and n = 4 results are properties of uniform directions in a plane and on a sphere, and the skew is the flatness of the cosine at its peak. It also makes the degrees of freedom self-evident — the subspace has dimension n − 1, and fitting the two means is what removed the other direction.

ask.q: Archimedes' theorem gives the n = 4 uniform result. What would the same argument give for n = 5, where the centred vectors live in four dimensions?
ask.nudge: The density is proportional to (1 − r²)^((d−3)/2) with d = 4. What shape is that?

scenes.title: Mastery test
scenes.objective: Demonstrate it independently, on questions you have not seen.
